transcript:
This is NPR News Now.
The latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Louise Schiavone.
International climate change negotiations in Turkey broke down in the final hours today,
failing to reach an agreement on how to limit global warming.
NPR's Lauren Summers reports.
The key sticking point was over fossil fuels.
Countries were negotiating an agreement to move away from using energy like coal and natural gas,
which produced heat-trapping emissions that warmed the planet.
Countries like Saudi Arabia rejected that language,
leading the European Union and others to walk out.
The U.S. was not at the negotiations.
Fossil fuels were part of a climate deal agreed to back in 2023.
Now some countries are questioning the value of the United Nations climate talks.
Most countries are not on track to meet their pledges to cut emissions.
Lauren Summer, NPR News.
The Port of Seattle is asking federal officials whether immigration agents followed airport protocol
during an operation at Seattle Tacoma International Airport this weekend.
Kate Stone from member station KUOW reports that ICE agents arrested two passengers on a packed jetway.
Witness video obtained by KUOW shows masked agents pulling two passengers out of the boarding line for the Los Angeles bound flight.
Security says ICE targeted Ricardo "Lorando" Mendoza and arrested Sofia Hernandez Meilla,
saying she threw hot coffee and will face a federal assault charge.
ICE says both are from Mexico and overstayed visas.
Passenger Aiden Mendoza, no relation, walked off the flight after watching what unfolded.
We want to help, but we're literally all trapped in this type of hallway, like we could get her as well.
Alaska Airlines and the Port of Seattle say they were not notified.
Port officials are reviewing whether DHS breached airport protocols.
For NPR News, I'm Kate Stone in Seattle.
In the Middle East, Palestinian officials and witnesses say that Israeli settlers set fires overnight in the Israeli-occupied West Bank.
They've been heavily criticized by a top Israeli politician.
NPR's Lauren Freya reports.
Video shows at least a dozen cars on fire and racist graffiti with the word "revenge" in Hebrew on Palestinian homes near Ramallah.
Israeli opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot calls it "Jewish terrorism in every sense of the word."
He blames extremist settlers who've set up illegal outposts in the area,
and accuses them of bringing the West Bank to the "brink of unchecked anarchy."
Eisenkot's leading coalition talks to oust Israel's far-right Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu,
who has extremist settlers in his cabinet.
Meanwhile, the United Nations says settler attacks on the Palestinian olive harvest hit a record high this year.
The UN accuses Netanyahu's government of not only failing to stop them, but of actively supporting them.
Lauren Freya, NPR News, Tel Aviv.
This is NPR.
Grand Theft Auto VI brought in nearly $3.8 billion worldwide on its first day.
It's the first new game in the series in 13 years.
Players can steal cars and pull up heists in the game.
As Vicky Barker reports from London, its release gave police an unexpected break in a real-life criminal case.
A police force in rural Bedfordshire was one of several around the world to ride on the promotional coattails of Grand Theft Auto VI.
Us cops, we gotta protect each other.
The force shared a series of wanted posters on Facebook using GTA-adjacent graphics,
featuring mugshots of six people under the heading "Bedfordshire's Most Wanted, Level 1-6."
The post generated thousands of likes and resulted in a tip-off that has now led to the arrest of one of the suspects wanted in connection with multiple burglaries and thefts.
One Facebook user commented, "Whoever's in charge of social media for Bedfordshire police needs a raise. This is legendary."
For NPR News, I'm Vicky Barker in London.
Delta Airlines is reporting flight delays today as it Atlantis Hub and other locations due to a problem with its automated weight and balance system.
This as the Thanksgiving travel week gets underway, Delta says it's using manual workarounds to move flights along as it works to restore automation.
Fourteen-year Denver Broncos pro-ESPN broadcast veteran Tom Jackson has died. The network announced Jackson's death. On Sunday, NFL countdown, he was 75.
I'm Louise Schiavone, NPR News, Washington.

topics.text: International climate talks in Turkey collapse over fossil fuel language, with Saudi Arabia rejecting it
Port of Seattle asks feds if ICE followed airport protocol in arrests of two passengers at SeaTac
Israeli opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot condemns settler arson attacks in West Bank near Ramallah
Grand Theft Auto VI earns nearly $3.8 billion worldwide on first day of release
Bedfordshire police's GTA-style wanted posters on Facebook lead to arrest of burglary suspect
Delta Airlines reports flight delays due to automated weight and balance system problem
ESPN broadcaster and former Denver Broncos player Tom Jackson dies at age 75
